claims.text: Malpractice needs: care below the ordinary standard of care, a professional relationship with the patient, and harm caused by that deviation.
claims.quote:
However, successful medical malpractice lawsuits require proof of the following:
The care provided was below the ordinary standard of care that would be provided by similar health care professionals under similar circumstances.
A professional relationship existed between the health care professional and the injured party.
The patient was harmed because of the deviation from the standard of care.

claims.text: Licensing board: patients can also file a complaint with the state licensing board.
claims.quote: When patients feel that their rights have been violated, they can complain to the state licensing board, instead of or in addition to bringing a lawsuit.

claims.text: Best defense: excellent care and trusting relationships with patients.
claims.quote: The best defense against malpractice lawsuits is providing excellent health care and building close, trusting, collaborative relationships with patients.

claims.text: Disclosing an error: tell the patient about every harmful error, why it happened, how its effects will be minimized, and how it will be prevented.
claims.quote:
Disclosure of all harmful errors
An explanation as to why the error occurred
How the error's effects will be minimized
Steps the physician (and organization) will take to prevent recurrences

claims.text: Full disclosure: also acknowledges responsibility and includes an apology.
claims.quote: "Full disclosure" of an error incorporates these components as well as acknowledgement of responsibility and an apology by the physician.

claims.text: Time-out (Universal Protocol): a planned pause with the whole team before starting, now required before any invasive procedure.
claims.quote: The concept of the surgical timeout—a planned pause before beginning the procedure in order to review important aspects of the procedure with all involved personnel—was developed to improve communication in the operating room and prevent WSPEs. The Universal Protocol also specifies use of a timeout prior to all procedures. Although initially designed for operating room procedures, timeouts are now required before any invasive procedure.
claims.locator: Preventing Wrong-Site, Wrong-Procedure, and Wrong-Patient Surgery

claims.text: Never events: wrong-patient, wrong-site, and wrong-procedure surgery (Joint Commission sentinel events).
claims.quote: Wrong-patient, wrong-site, and wrong-procedure errors are all considered never events by the National Quality Forum, and are considered sentinel events by The Joint Commission.
